Speculation

/spek-yuh-LAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Speculation means the forming of theories or guesses about something without firm evidence

Speculation means the forming of theories or guesses about something without firm evidence

Worked Example

When the star quarterback skipped practice twice in one week, the hallways filled with <strong style="color:var(--accent);">speculation</strong> — some said he was injured, others said he was transferring, but nobody actually knew anything.

Everyone is building theories — injury, transfer — while the sentence tells us plainly that nobody has any real information. Theories multiplying in the absence of evidence is exactly what speculation is.

How Speculation Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

conjecture

conjecture: an opinion formed without proof

guesswork

guesswork: the process of making guesses

supposition

supposition: something assumed to be true without proof

Antonyms

certainty

certainty: the state of being completely sure, beyond doubt

fact

fact: something known to be true

How Strong Is It? — wondering → speculation → fantasy

wondering vs. speculation

wondering vs. speculation: Wondering is idle and open — you're just musing, with no theory in mind; speculation actively builds explanations even though the evidence isn't there.

fantasy vs. speculation

fantasy vs. speculation: Fantasy goes further than speculation — it lets go of evidence entirely and imagines freely, with no expectation of being true at all.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of speculation.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — specul-

Root — specul-: to spy out, observe from a watchtower (Latin speculari, from specere 'to look at')

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Speculation began as 'keeping watch from a lookout' — scanning the horizon for what might come. The Latin root specere means 'to look at,' and today speculation means mentally scanning the possibilities when solid evidence isn't in view.

Use the root in a new word: spectacle

Use the root in a new word: spectacle: A spectacle is something striking to look at — the fireworks finale over the bay was a spectacle the whole town came out to see.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / Journalistic

Speculation often travels with dismissive partners: 'pure speculation,' 'mere speculation,' 'idle speculation' — phrases writers use to wave away unproven claims. SAT reading passages also use its finance sense: risky investing based on guesses about future prices. Keep it distinct from prediction, a related word in this unit: a prediction is a committed, stated forecast (often evidence-based); speculation is open guessing with little or no evidence.
